title: Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME) Part One: Format of Internet Message Bodies
subtitle: How plain-text email learned to carry pictures, other alphabets and attachments.
summary: MIME extends the RFC 822 email format without breaking it. Five new header fields, MIME-Version, Content-Type, Content-Transfer-Encoding and the optional Content-ID and Content-Description, label what a message body contains and how it was encoded for transport. Binary data is wrapped in either quoted-printable or base64 so it survives mail systems that only handle short lines of 7-bit ASCII.

eli5.summary: Mail pipes were built to carry only plain letters, so MIME puts a label on every parcel saying what is inside and how it was wrapped, and the wrapping turns anything, even a photo, into plain letters that fit through the pipe.

questions: what does content-type mean in an email

tldr.problem: Internet mail, as defined by RFC 822, carried only short lines of 7-bit US-ASCII text, with no way to send images, audio, other alphabets or several parts in one message.
tldr.mechanism: New header fields label the body with a media type (Content-Type) and say how it was encoded (Content-Transfer-Encoding), and two encodings, quoted-printable and base64, turn arbitrary bytes into safe 7-bit text.
tldr.outcome: Every modern email client still builds and reads messages this way, which is how attachments, HTML mail and non-English text travel over a transport that never changed.

today: MIME is the format of essentially all email. Every message with an attachment, an HTML body or a non-English subject uses the headers defined here, and mail clients such as Thunderbird, Apple Mail and Outlook encode and decode base64 and quoted-printable automatically. The same Content-Type idea (media types, also called MIME types) was reused by HTTP and by file-type registries, so image/png and text/html are familiar well outside email. RFC 2045 has been amended since, for example by RFC 2231 for parameter encoding and RFC 6532 for internationalized headers.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Since 1982 RFC 822 had defined the format of Internet text messages, and it said nothing about message bodies beyond treating them as flat US-ASCII text. As the Internet grew, three limits became painful: no way to send audio, video or images; no way to write text in languages that need more than US-ASCII; and a transport (SMTP, RFC 821) limited to short lines of 7-bit characters, which the RFC puts at 1000 characters or less.

Users worked around this with ad hoc tools such as uuencode, but there was no standard way to tell the receiver which tool had been used. Gateways to X.400, which could carry non-text material, had to either convert it to text or discard it.

MIME, the Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions, is a set of five documents. This first one defines the header fields. RFC 2046 defines media types, RFC 2047 non-ASCII text in headers, RFC 2048 registration procedures, and RFC 2049 conformance. This document obsoletes RFC 1521, RFC 1522 and RFC 1590.

The authors warn that some mechanisms "may seem somewhat strange or even baroque" and explain that "compatibility was always favored over elegance."
sections.eli5: The mail system was built like a pipe that only lets plain letters through. People wanted to send pictures and songs, and to write in many alphabets, but nobody could tell what a strange parcel was. MIME is the plan for labelling parcels so the pipe never has to change.

sections.title: Definitions and vocabulary
sections.content:
Section 2 fixes the words used by the whole MIME set. The one that matters most is the entity: the MIME header fields plus the content of either a whole message or one part of a multipart message. The body of an entity is its content. The RFC admits these definitions are circular, because "the overall structure of a MIME message is indeed recursive."

It also defines three kinds of data by what a transport may carry:

7bit data
Lines of 998 octets or less between CRLFs, no octet above 127, no NULs, and CR and LF only as part of CRLF.
8bit data
Same line rules, but octets above 127 are allowed. NULs are still forbidden.
Binary data
Any sequence of octets whatsoever.

A "character set" in MIME means a method of converting octets into characters, and its definition must fully specify the mapping, with no external profiling information. All media type, subtype and parameter names are case-insensitive, but parameter values are case-sensitive unless said otherwise.
sections.eli5: Before labelling parcels you need words for them. An entity is any parcel, even one inside a bigger parcel. Seven-bit stuff is the simplest kind of parcel, eight-bit stuff is a bit fancier, and binary can be anything at all.

sections.title: MIME header fields and MIME-Version
sections.content:
MIME defines new RFC 822 header fields that describe an entity. They can appear in two places: the ordinary header of a message, and the header of a body part inside a multipart body. Only fields whose names begin with "Content-" have any MIME meaning in a body part header.

The first field is MIME-Version. Messages composed in accordance with this document MUST include it with the verbatim text MIME-Version: 1.0. Its presence is an assertion that the message complies, and a value other than 1.0 cannot be assumed to conform. It is required at the top level of a message but not for each body part, and an embedded message/rfc822 needs one only if that embedded message claims to be MIME.

RFC 822 comments inside the field are ignored, so these four are equivalent: 1.0, 1.0 (produced by MetaSend Vx.x), (produced by MetaSend Vx.x) 1.0 and 1.(produced by MetaSend Vx.x)0.

Without a MIME-Version a receiver may interpret the body by local convention. The RFC notes that non-MIME mail can contain "just about anything," such as a uuencoded tar file.
sections.eli5: MIME-Version is the sticker on the front that says "this parcel follows the labelling plan." If the sticker is missing, the receiver has to guess what is inside.

sections.title: Content-Type
sections.content:
The Content-Type field describes the body well enough that a mail reader can choose how to show or handle it. Its value is a media type: a type and a subtype separated by a slash, followed by any number of ;attribute=value parameters. The subtype is mandatory and has no default. Matching of type, subtype and attribute names is always case-insensitive.

The top-level type tells a reader the general kind of data even when it does not know the subtype. The five discrete types are text, image, audio, video and application. The two composite types, which contain other entities, are message and multipart. Their details are in RFC 2046. Private subtypes start with "X-", while standard ones are registered with IANA as described in RFC 2048.

Parameters modify the subtype. For example charset applies to any text subtype and boundary is required for any multipart subtype. Receivers must ignore parameters they do not recognize. Values that contain a tspecial such as /, =, ? or @ must be written as a quoted-string.

If no Content-Type is present, the default is text/plain; charset=us-ascii, and the RFC recommends assuming the same default when the field is syntactically invalid.
sections.eli5: Content-Type is the label that says "photo," "song" or "letter," plus a more exact kind like "PNG photo." If you do not know the exact kind you can still tell it is a photo and not a song.

sections.title: Content-Transfer-Encoding
sections.content:
Many useful media types are naturally 8-bit or binary, but SMTP restricts mail to 7-bit US-ASCII with lines no longer than 1000 characters including the CRLF. The Content-Transfer-Encoding field says how the body was transformed to fit, so the receiver knows what decoding to apply.

The value is one token: 7bit, 8bit, binary, quoted-printable or base64, or an X- token. Values are case-insensitive, and 7bit is assumed if the field is absent. The field carries two facts: which transformation was used, and what domain the result is in. The first three values mean no transformation has happened and only label the domain. Quoted-printable and base64 convert arbitrary input into the 7bit range.

Several rules follow. The label must be truthful: 8-bit data cannot be called 7bit. A multipart entity may use only 7bit, 8bit or binary (some message subtypes are even more restricted), so that encoding is applied at the innermost level and never nested. An entity with an unrecognized encoding must be treated as application/octet-stream. Creating new encodings is "STRONGLY discouraged."

The RFC says there are no standardized Internet mail transports where unencoded binary data is legitimate, so the binary value is not actually valid in Internet mail.
sections.eli5: This label tells how the parcel was wrapped so it could squeeze through the pipe. The receiver reads the label and unwraps it. You may wrap a parcel once, but never wrap a wrapped parcel.

sections.title: Quoted-printable encoding
sections.content:
Quoted-printable is meant for data that is mostly printable US-ASCII, so the encoded form stays readable. It works with five rules:

Rule 1: =XX
Any octet may be written as "=" and two uppercase hex digits, for example =3D for the equals sign and =0C for form feed. Lowercase digits are not allowed.
Rule 2: literal
Octets 33 to 60 and 62 to 126 may appear as themselves.
Rule 3: white space
Tab (9) and space (32) may appear literally but never at the end of a line, where they must use rule 1.
Rule 4: line breaks
A CRLF line break in text is written as a CRLF. In non-text data, CR and LF must be written as =0D and =0A.
Rule 5: soft breaks
Encoded lines are at most 76 characters. An "=" as the last character of a line is a soft break that is removed on decoding.

The 76-character limit excludes the CRLF but includes any equal signs. Decoders must delete trailing white space on a line, since transports may have added it. Because a hyphen can appear as itself, a multipart boundary containing "=_" can never appear in a quoted-printable body. The RFC also lists illegal strings and suggests how a robust decoder might handle them, such as accepting =3d as =3D.
sections.eli5: Quoted-printable leaves ordinary letters alone and writes only the odd ones as an equals sign plus a code. A message that is mostly normal still looks normal. If a line is too long, you end it with an equals sign to say "keep reading, the sentence continues."

sections.title: Base64 encoding
sections.content:
Base64 is the dense, uniform choice for data that is not humanly readable. It reads the input three octets (24 bits) at a time and splits them into four 6-bit groups. Each group is an index into a table of 64 printable characters: A to Z are 0 to 25, a to z are 26 to 51, 0 to 9 are 52 to 61, + is 62 and / is 63. The alphabet avoids characters with special meaning to SMTP, such as the period, and the hyphen used by multipart boundaries. Because every 3 bytes become 4 characters, the output is only about 33 percent larger than the input.

If fewer than 24 bits remain at the end, zero bits are added on the right to make whole 6-bit groups, and the "=" character pads the result to a multiple of 4. One leftover octet becomes two characters followed by "==", and two leftover octets become three characters followed by "=".

Encoded lines must be no longer than 76 characters. Decoders ignore line breaks and any character outside the alphabet, though stray characters probably indicate a transmission error. Text must be converted to CRLF line breaks before encoding.

The RFC says base64 is virtually identical to the encoding used in Privacy Enhanced Mail (RFC 1421).
sections.eli5: Base64 chops any parcel into small pieces and spells each piece with just 64 safe letters and symbols. It makes the parcel a bit bigger, but everything spelled this way gets through the pipe, even a picture.

sections.title: Content-ID, Content-Description and security
sections.content:
Two optional fields round out the set. Content-ID has the same syntax as Message-ID and labels an entity with a world-unique identifier so that one body can refer to another. It is mandatory for implementations that generate message/external-body, so that fetched data can be cached. Content-Description is free text, always optional, presumed to be US-ASCII unless RFC 2047 encoding is used; the RFC's example is "a picture of the Space Shuttle Endeavor."

Future header fields that describe content should begin with "Content-", so that they can be told apart from ordinary RFC 822 fields. This is the MIME-extension-field rule.

The Security Considerations section is a single sentence: security issues are discussed in the second document of the set, RFC 2046. The appendix collects the complete BNF grammar for the document, which refers back to RFC 822 for terms it does not define.
sections.eli5: Content-ID is a name tag so one parcel can point at another. Content-Description is a sticky note in plain words, like "birthday photo." The grown-up rules about safety are in the next document.
